content: Overactive bladder syndrome affects a significant proportion of adults, with symptoms such as urgency, frequency, and urgency urinary incontinence. Anticholinergic drugs are commonly used to manage these symptoms. This study aimed to compare the effects of different anticholinergic drugs and their dosages in adults with overactive bladder symptoms or detrusor overactivity. Tolterodine versus Oxybutynin: When comparing tolterodine and oxybutynin, there were no statistically significant differences in terms of quality of life, patient-reported cure or improvement, leakage episodes, or the number of voids in 24 hours. However, tolterodine was associated with fewer withdrawals due to adverse events (risk ratio [RR] 0.52, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.40 to 0.66) and a lower risk of dry mouth (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.71). Solifenacin versus Tolterodine: Solifenacin demonstrated statistically significant advantages over tolterodine in several areas, including quality of life (standardized mean difference [SMD] -0.12, 95% CI -0.23 to -0.01), patient-reported cure or improvement (RR 1.25, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.39), fewer leakage episodes in 24 hours (weighted mean difference [WMD] -0.30, 95% CI -0.53 to -0.08), and fewer urgency episodes in 24 hours (WMD -0.43, 95% CI -0.74 to -0.13). There was no significant difference in withdrawals due to adverse events or dry mouth. However, after sensitivity analysis, solifenacin was associated with a statistically significant lower risk of dry mouth compared to immediate-release tolterodine (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.94). Fesoterodine versus Extended-Release Tolterodine: Fesoterodine showed statistically significant improvements in quality of life (SMD -0.20, 95% CI -0.27 to -0.14), patient-reported cure or improvement (RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.16), fewer leakage episodes (WMD -0.19, 95% CI -0.30 to -0.09), reduced frequency (WMD -0.27, 95% CI -0.47 to -0.06), and fewer urgency episodes (WMD -0.44, 95% CI -0.72 to -0.16) in 24 hours. However, fesoterodine was associated with a higher risk of withdrawal due to adverse events (RR 1.45, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.98) and a higher risk of dry mouth (RR 1.80, 95% CI 1.58 to 2.05) at 12 weeks. Different Doses of Tolterodine: The standard starting dose of tolterodine (2 mg twice daily) was compared to lower doses (0.5 mg and 1 mg twice daily) and a higher dose (4 mg twice daily). The 1 mg, 2 mg, and 4 mg doses had similar effects on leakage episodes and micturitions in 24 hours. However, the 2 mg and 4 mg doses were associated with a greater risk of dry mouth at two to 12 weeks. Different Doses of Solifenacin: The standard starting dose of solifenacin (5 mg once daily) was compared to 10 mg once daily. The 10 mg dose was more effective in reducing frequency and urgency but was associated with a higher risk of dry mouth at four to 12 weeks. Different Doses of Fesoterodine: The recommended starting dose of fesoterodine (4 mg once daily) was compared to 8 mg and 12 mg doses. The 8 mg dose showed better clinical efficacy (patient-reported cure, fewer leakage episodes, and fewer micturitions in 24 hours) than the 4 mg dose but was associated with a higher risk of dry mouth. There was no significant difference in efficacy between the 4 mg and 12 mg doses, but the 12 mg dose had a significantly higher risk of dry mouth at eight to 12 weeks. Extended-Release versus Immediate-Release Preparations of Oxybutynin or Tolterodine: There were no statistically significant differences in cure or improvement, leakage episodes, micturitions in 24 hours, or withdrawals due to adverse events between extended-release and immediate-release preparations. However, extended-release preparations were associated with a lower risk of dry mouth at two to 12 weeks. One Extended-Release Preparation versus Another: Oral extended-release tolterodine was associated with a lower risk of dry mouth compared to oral extended-release oxybutynin (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.95). There was no significant difference between transdermal oxybutynin and oral extended-release tolterodine, although some individuals withdrew due to skin reactions at the transdermal patch site at 12 weeks. Authors' Conclusions: When choosing between oral immediate-release oxybutynin and tolterodine, tolterodine may be preferred due to a reduced risk of dry mouth. For tolterodine, the standard starting dose is 2 mg twice daily, but a 1 mg twice daily dose may be equally effective with a lower risk of dry mouth. Extended-release preparations of oxybutynin or tolterodine may be preferred over immediate-release formulations due to a lower risk of dry mouth. Between solifenacin and immediate-release tolterodine, solifenacin may be preferred for better efficacy and a lower risk of dry mouth. The standard starting dose of solifenacin is 5 mg once daily, which can be increased to 10 mg once daily for improved efficacy, albeit with an increased risk of dry mouth. Between fesoterodine and extended-release tolterodine, fesoterodine may be preferred for superior efficacy, but it carries a higher risk of withdrawal due to adverse events and a higher risk of dry mouth. There is limited evidence regarding quality of life, costs, or long-term outcomes in these studies. Data on other anticholinergic drugs were insufficient to draw conclusions.
